content.text: Looking at this change, it's a UI refactor for a macOS SwiftUI/AppKit app: replacing a floating `NSPanel` theme picker with a toolbar-anchored `.popover`. Let me verify the scope by checking the actual files for anything security-relevant.

1	import AppKit
2	import SwiftUI
3	
4	/// Layout constants for the custom title bar. The bar is drawn as the top strip of the window's
5	/// (full-size) content rather than in an `NSTitlebarAccessoryViewController` — a leading accessory
6	/// is clamped to the native ~32pt title-bar height and can't be made taller (verified), so the
7	/// Chrome/Arc approach is used instead: `.fullSizeContentView` + draw the bar in content at any
8	/// height. Tune `height` to taste.
9	enum WorkroomTitlebar {
10	  /// Standard title-bar height. The custom bar is now a `.left` titlebar accessory, which AppKit
11	  /// clamps to the standard title-bar height; this constant is used as the reorder-vs-drop threshold
12	  /// in `RootView.workroomChipLocal` (a chip drag staying within the bar strip is a reorder). ~28pt.
13	  static let height: CGFloat = 28
14	  /// Leading inset so the bar's first control clears the traffic-light cluster.
15	  static let trafficLightInset: CGFloat = 80
16	}
17	
18	/// A transparent backing view that lets a click-drag on the empty parts of the custom title bar
19	/// move the window — the content area isn't window-draggable by default (only the real title bar
20	/// is), so the bar needs this to stay draggable. Interactive controls drawn on top consume their
21	/// own clicks; clicks that fall through to this view start a window drag.
22	struct WindowDragBackground: NSViewRepresentable {
23	  func makeNSView(context: Context) -> NSView { DragView() }
24	  func updateNSView(_ nsView: NSView, context: Context) {}
25	
26	  final class DragView: NSView {
27	    override var mouseDownCanMoveWindow: Bool { true }
28	    override func mouseDown(with event: NSEvent) {
29	      // Double-click on the empty bar runs the system title-bar action (zoom/minimize); a single
30	      // click-drag moves the window.
31	      if event.clickCount == 2 {
32	        window?.performZoom(nil)
33	      } else {
34	        window?.performDrag(with: event)
35	      }
36	    }
37	  }
38	}
39	
40	/// Toggles the window's `isMovable` to gate AppKit's automatic title-bar drag. The custom title bar
41	/// (issue #23) is drawn in the window's full-size content, where AppKit's title-bar drag ignores the
42	/// content views' `mouseDownCanMoveWindow` (verified) — so a drag anywhere in the bar, including on a
43	/// workroom tab chip, moves the whole *window* and steals the chip's reorder `DragGesture`. `isMovable`
44	/// is the one lever that actually disables that drag, but it's window-wide, so we flip it by hover:
45	/// the bar passes `movable = false` only while the cursor is over (or dragging) a chip, and `true`
46	/// otherwise — so the chips reorder while the empty bar still drags the window. Hover fires before the
47	/// press, so the flag is already set when the drag begins.
48	struct WindowMovableController: NSViewRepresentable {
49	  let movable: Bool
50	
51	  func makeNSView(context: Context) -> NSView {
52	    let view = NSView(frame: .zero)
53	    DispatchQueue.main.async { [weak view] in view?.window?.isMovable = movable }
54	    return view
55	  }
56	
57	  func updateNSView(_ nsView: NSView, context: Context) {
58	    nsView.window?.isMovable = movable
59	  }
60	}
61	
62	/// The single unified title-bar toolbar, split into a leading and a trailing half hosted as
63	/// `NSTitlebarAccessoryViewController`s (see `TitlebarAccessory`). They sit in the window's *one*
64	/// title-bar row — the leading half right after the traffic lights, the trailing half at the
65	/// window's true trailing edge — so together they span the full width with the draggable title-bar
66	/// gap between them.
67	///
68	/// Why accessories rather than `.toolbar`: SwiftUI's `.toolbar` placement is column-scoped in a
69	/// `NavigationSplitView` (`.primaryAction` docks to a column, not the window edge), and `.toolbar`
70	/// items render with the framework's own chrome. Hosting plain SwiftUI `HStack`s in title-bar
71	/// accessories instead gives every control one shared `.borderless` style and exact placement,
72	/// independent of the split's columns.
73	
74	/// A hairline group separator shared by the title-bar bars.
75	struct TitlebarDivider: View {
76	  private let theme = ThemeService.shared
77	
78	  var body: some View {
79	    Rectangle()
80	      .fill(theme.tokens.border)
81	      .frame(width: 1, height: 14)
82	      .padding(.horizontal, 4)
83	  }
84	}
85	
86	/// Leading title-bar controls: sidebar toggle + history nav (issue #26). Our
87	/// own sidebar toggle (leftmost, right after the traffic lights) replaces NavigationSplitView's auto
88	/// one. `.toolbar(removing:)` is meant to drop it, but doesn't fully take, so the window toolbar is
89	/// hidden outright in `WindowBackgroundThemer` to kill its "more toolbar items" overflow chevron.
90	struct LeadingTitlebarBar: View {
91	  @EnvironmentObject var store: AppStore
92	
93	  var body: some View {
94	    HStack(spacing: 6) {
95	      Button {
96	        store.sidebarVisible.toggle()
97	      } label: {
98	        Image(systemName: "sidebar.left")
99	      }
100	      .help(store.sidebarVisible ? "Hide sidebar (⌃⌘S)" : "Show sidebar (⌃⌘S)")
101	      .accessibilityLabel("Toggle sidebar")
102	      .accessibilityIdentifier("toolbar.toggleSidebar")
103	      // Hovering this button (while the sidebar is collapsed) peeks the sidebar via the edge-reveal
104	      // overlay (issue #74) — the trigger is the button alone, never the toolbar strip that used to
105	      // sit above the workroom tabs. Only report while collapsed so a hover with the sidebar pinned
106	      // doesn't churn reveal state.
107	      .onHover { hovering in
108	        if !store.sidebarVisible { store.hoveringLeftToggle = hovering }
109	      }
110	
111	      TitlebarDivider()
112	
113	      // The two identifiers below are a deliberate hook with no test behind them yet: the nav UI test
114	      // drives ⌘[/⌘] instead, because these buttons live in an AppKit titlebar accessory that no
115	      // XCUITest has ever queried, and a tap on a `.disabled` one fails silently (a green test proving
116	      // nothing). Kept so a future titlebar test has a handle. `accessibilityLabel` is what assistive
117	      // tech actually reads.
118	      Button {
119	        store.navigateBack()
120	      } label: {
121	        Image(systemName: "chevron.left")
122	      }
123	      .help("Back (⌘[)")
124	      .accessibilityLabel("Back")
125	      .accessibilityIdentifier("toolbar.navigateBack")
126	      .disabled(!store.canGoBack)
127	
128	      Button {
129	        store.navigateForward()
130	      } label: {
131	        Image(systemName: "chevron.right")
132	      }
133	      .help("Forward (⌘])")
134	      .accessibilityLabel("Forward")
135	      .accessibilityIdentifier("toolbar.navigateForward")
136	      .disabled(!store.canGoForward)
137	    }
138	    .buttonStyle(ToolbarIconButtonStyle())
139	    .padding(.horizontal, 10)
140	    // The titlebar accessory host is the full title-bar height (52pt — NOT 28), and NSHostingView
141	    // top-aligns a fixed-height root inside it, so the icons sat high. Fill the host and let the HStack
142	    // centre its buttons on the traffic-light line (the close button centres at y=26 of the 52pt host).
143	    .frame(maxHeight: .infinity)
144	  }
145	}
146	
147	/// Trailing title-bar controls: the update pill and the quick terminal (issue #39) — both
148	/// **window-level**, which is now the whole point. Everything workroom-scoped has left: notifications
149	/// and inspector visibility moved to the activity bar, and issue #139 moved the selected target's
150	/// run/open-in actions into each workroom pane's own title bar, where a co-displayed split member's
151	/// are reachable too. With no update pending this collapses to just the quick terminal.
152	struct TrailingTitlebarBar: View {
153	  @EnvironmentObject var updater: Updater
154	  @EnvironmentObject var store: AppStore
155	
156	  /// The theme dropdown (issue #36), anchored to its own toolbar button.
157	  ///
158	  /// Window-local `@State`, like the sheets `RootView` owns: the `Theme…` command's notification is
159	  /// broadcast to every window, and the key-window guard below is what decides which one opens.
160	  @State private var showThemePicker = false
161	
162	  var body: some View {
163	    HStack(spacing: 6) {
164	      // A newer version is waiting (Sparkle gentle reminder) — the accent pill leads the trailing
165	      // controls. Self-hides when no update is pending; the divider matches. It lives here, not in the
166	      // leading bar, because there it overran the sidebar and sat on the NavigationSplitView's
167	      // sidebar/detail divider, whose full-height resize grab zone stole the cursor (and a drag
168	      // resized the sidebar). At the window's trailing edge it's nowhere near that divider.
169	      if updater.availableVersionString != nil {
170	        UpdateAvailableButton()
171	        TitlebarDivider()
172	      }
173	
174	      // Theme (⌘⇧K) — a dropdown anchored here rather than a sheet or a window of its own, because
175	      // picking a theme is a live-preview gesture: ↑/↓ apply families as you move through them, so the
176	      // app behind the dropdown IS the preview. A sheet made that impossible twice over (measured on
177	      // the real build): its modality had AppKit render the whole window inactive — traffic lights
178	      // greyed, the sidebar's VCS dot badges orange → dull brown — and being anchored under the title
179	      // bar it sat on top of the content whose colours you were choosing, with nothing to drag.
180	      //
181	      // A popover is transient, so it needs no dismiss affordance and no modal bookkeeping: clicking
182	      // anywhere else closes it, and anything that raises a dialog closes it too (below). It is
183	      // therefore deliberately absent from `AppStore.hasModalPresentation`.
184	      Button {
185	        showThemePicker.toggle()
186	      } label: {
187	        Image(systemName: "paintpalette")
188	      }
189	      .help("Theme (⌘⇧K)")
190	      .accessibilityLabel("Theme")
191	      .accessibilityIdentifier("toolbar.theme")
192	      .popover(isPresented: $showThemePicker, arrowEdge: .bottom) { ThemePicker() }
193	
194	      // Quick Terminal (⌥§) — a ~/ shell in its own window. Always present, and since issue #139 moved
195	      // the selected target's run/open-in actions into the workroom pane title bars, the only control
196	      // left at the window's trailing edge besides the update pill.
197	      Button {
198	        NotificationCenter.default.post(name: .showQuickTerminal, object: nil)
199	      } label: {
200	        // The `.badge.plus` extends this glyph's box upward, so a plain centre sits ~0.5pt high vs the
201	        // other icons; nudge it down to sit on the same line.
202	        Image(systemName: "macwindow.badge.plus")
203	          .offset(y: 0.5)
204	      }
205	      .help("Quick Terminal (⌥§)")
206	      .accessibilityLabel("Quick Terminal")
207	      .accessibilityIdentifier("toolbar.quickTerminal")
208	    }
209	    .buttonStyle(ToolbarIconButtonStyle())
210	    // Trailing gap so the last control isn't flush to the window edge (previously supplied by the
211	    // removed TitlebarControlsBar — the right-sidebar toggle it hosted is redundant with the activity
212	    // bar, whose section icons show/collapse the inspector).
213	    .padding(.trailing, 10)
214	    // Fill the full-height (52pt) accessory host so the HStack centres its buttons — see LeadingTitlebarBar.
215	    .frame(maxHeight: .infinity)
216	    // The `Theme…` command (⌘⇧K) can't anchor a popover from a menu, so it posts and this bar — which
217	    // owns the anchor — presents. Guarded on the key window because the post reaches every window's
218	    // accessory; toggling means the shortcut closes the dropdown as well as opening it.
219	    .onReceive(NotificationCenter.default.publisher(for: .showThemePicker)) { _ in
220	      guard store.hostWindow?.isKeyWindow ?? false else { return }
221	      showThemePicker.toggle()
222	    }
223	    // "Anything else closes it." A popover dismisses itself on a click outside, but a *keyboard* command
224	    // never sends that click — so the two things a command can do to this window close it explicitly: put
225	    // a dialog or sheet up (a dropdown hanging over a modal is confusing and unreachable past), and move
226	    // the selection (⌘1–9, ⌥⌘digit, the switchers), which is the action a stale dropdown would most
227	    // obviously be sitting on top of.
228	    .onChange(of: store.hasModalPresentation) { _, blocked in
229	      if blocked { showThemePicker = false }
230	    }
231	    .onChange(of: store.selectedTargetID) { _, _ in showThemePicker = false }
232	  }
233	}

content.text:
This change is a pure UI refactor — it replaces a floating `NSPanel` theme picker with a SwiftUI `.popover` anchored to a toolbar button. I traced every touched file:

- **`AppStore.swift`**: only a comment update about which sheets participate in `hasModalPresentation`. No logic change.
- **`ThemePanel.swift`**: deleted (was an `NSPanel` subclass; no security-sensitive sinks).
- **`ThemeService.swift`**: only a doc comment on the `showThemePicker` notification name.
- **`KeyboardShortcutsView.swift`**: only comment updates.
- **`RootView.swift`**: only a comment update.
- **`ThemePicker.swift`**: removes an optional `onDone` closure and the branching `close()`; both hosts now use SwiftUI's `dismiss`. Adds `.onExitCommand { dismiss() }`. Pure UI.
- **`TitlebarBars.swift`**: adds a `Button` + `.popover` bound to `@State private var showThemePicker`. Observes `.showThemePicker` (process-local `NotificationCenter`, not attacker-influenceable — same trust boundary as other in-process signals). Auto-closes on `hasModalPresentation` or `selectedTargetID` change.
- **`WorkroomApp.swift`**: removes app-level `ThemePanelController.shared.attach()` and adds `.disabled(modalBlocked)` to the `Theme…` menu item (tightens rather than loosens).
- **Test files**: only touch `UserDefaults` in the developer's own domain in test-only setUp/tearDown paths; no production behavior.

No sinks introduced/removed: no shell/exec, no SQL, no filesystem paths from untrusted input, no outbound HTTP, no HTML, no deserialization, no template rendering, no IPC from a less-privileged process, no auth/RBAC, no allowlists, no crypto, no logging of PII/secrets, no cache directives, no dynamic loader. The one "external" signal (`NotificationCenter` posts) is process-local and already used by many other UI commands. `Defaults[.themeFamily]` is a user preference driven by UI clicks.

Nothing crosses a trust boundary; nothing gains or drops a security-relevant guard. The `.disabled(modalBlocked)` on the `Theme…` command is a net UX/robustness improvement, not a regression.
